HISTORY & PHYSICAL (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
33-year-old engineer with childhood-onset asthma presents with 2–3 days of wheeze, exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, and subjective fever; clinical impression is an acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by viral infection or allergens.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Wheezing and shortness of breath.  
• Onset/duration: Began 2–3 days ago; abrupt onset.  
• Course: Persistent over last few days; limits walking to work, occasionally unable to finish sentences; currently feels well at rest.  
• Provocative / relieving factors: Symptoms mainly on exertion (walking); rest improves breathing.  
• Associated symptoms: Dry cough; patient “thought” she had fever but measured 37 °C.  No chest pain, no sputum, no haemoptysis, no nocturnal breathlessness.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives): No chest pain, no palpitations, no syncope, no leg swelling, no upper-respiratory congestion, no sore throat.  

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – onset in childhood, severe enough to require occasional hospital visits (never ICU). Stopped regular medication ~3–4 years ago; currently uses salbutamol inhaler PRN every few weeks and before exercise.  
• Hay fever (allergic rhinitis) – untreated.  
• Eczema – historical.  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.  

Medications:
• Salbutamol inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented (patient uses PRN every few weeks; will increase as per plan).  
• No regular antihistamines or other drugs.  

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Lives with partner.  
• Occupation: Engineer; currently working from home or on sick leave due to dyspnoea.  
• Smoking: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol: ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days.  
• Recreational drugs: Not mentioned.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
Tele-consult only.  
• Reported temperature: 37 °C.  
• No additional vitals or physical findings documented.

Investigations:
• None to date; peak-flow monitoring to be initiated.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation  
– Plan:  
  • Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 h via spacer.  
  • Prescribe spacer device; pharmacist to demonstrate correct technique.  
  • Prescribe peak-flow meter; patient to record readings morning and evening for 1 week.  
  • Safety-net: Call back urgently if temperature rises or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens.

Issue 2: Under-controlled baseline asthma  
– Plan:  
  • Arrange follow-up review in 1 week (or sooner if deterioration) to assess peak-flow diary and consider addition of maintenance inhaler (e.g., inhaled corticosteroid) per asthma guidelines.

Issue 3: Atopic symptoms (hay fever)  
– Plan:  
  • Start regular oral antihistamine (OTC; specific agent/dose not documented) to reduce allergen-induced airway irritation.  
  • Education on allergen avoidance.

General advice:  
• Continue working from home until exercise tolerance improves.  
• Monitor ability to speak full sentences and perform activities of daily living; seek urgent care if deterioration.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute asthma exacerbation – High likelihood: Known asthma, classic wheeze/dyspnoea, responds to bronchodilator plan.  
2. Viral respiratory tract infection / acute bronchitis – Moderate likelihood: Acute onset, dry cough, subjective fever; could have triggered asthma.  
3. Allergic (pollen-induced) asthma flare – Moderate likelihood: Atopic history; no overt infection signs, season not specified.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing elements: No blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, or oxygen saturation recorded; allergy and medication doses incomplete; no family history obtained.  
• Conflicts: Patient reported “fever”; objective temperature normal (37 °C) – conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional interruptions but clinically adequate.
